Official learning objectives

  1. Apply occupation-based interventions in management of hand/upper-extremity conditions.
  2. Discuss the utilization of splinting and adaptive equipment used by occupational therapists to facilitate symptom improvement and performance of life tasks and occupations.
  3. Recognize the role of occupational therapy as part of interprofessional collaborative management of hand/upper-extremity conditions.

Big picture

Occupational need → five-domain assessment → appropriate intervention → functional participation, with ongoing physician coordination, especially after surgery. The lecture’s cases ask you to choose therapy based on context—not just to name a diagnosis.

OT FOR HAND PROBLEMS · 01

Occupation-based rehabilitation: the functional goal

Occupational therapy (OT) is not simply a sequence of isolated hand exercises. Its stated purpose is restoring participation in meaningful occupations—such as dressing, meal preparation, work, childcare, and hobbies. Upper-quarter rehabilitation supports healing and surgical outcomes, restores patient factors, and improves the quality of movement.

Dr. Hall sets a pragmatic treatment goal: return to usual activities without pain or with limited pain (the lecture gives <3/10 as an example). Pain scores matter, but function and task participation ultimately determine whether the treatment is useful.

The five foundational domains

  1. Pain—is movement tolerable enough to participate?
  2. Range of motion (ROM)—can the joint traverse the motion the task requires?
  3. Strength—can it generate/hold enough force?
  4. Edema—is swelling restricting motion or causing ache?
  5. Sensation, coordination, and dexterity—can the person sense and control objects safely?
MUST KNOW

These five domains define OT evaluation and intervention throughout the cases. The right treatment depends on which functional factors are impaired.

RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · Why might increasing grip strength alone fail to improve independence?

Pain, edema, restricted ROM, sensory loss or poor dexterity may still block the actual occupation. OT evaluates all five domains and the task context.

OT FOR HAND PROBLEMS · 02

Reducing pain without losing function

Lecture options: moist heat, fluidotherapy, cold compresses; therapeutic exercise (nerve glides for nerve pain or support-muscle strengthening for tendinitis); therapeutic massage for spasms; desensitization for nerve hypersensitivity; adaptive equipment for task compensation.

Reasoning: if tissue is painful and sensitive, gripping harder can increase distress and lead to avoidance. An intervention may reduce symptom burden, while a larger-handled utensil changes the load required for the same task. Pain management thus combines remediation with compensation, rather than assuming that every patient can immediately return to full loading.

CLINICAL CONNECTION

A patient with painful fine-motor activity may benefit from a tool modification even while underlying pain is being treated.

RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · A patient with neuropathic hand hypersensitivity struggles to hold utensils. Which two distinct OT strategies could help?

Desensitization for nerve hypersensitivity and adaptive equipment to make eating easier while recovery continues.

OT FOR HAND PROBLEMS · 03

Restoring ROM: active, assisted, passive, and scar-directed work

ToolPrimary purpose in the lecture
AROMPatient moves the joint actively.
AAROMPatient moves with assistance to reach available motion.
PROMExternal force moves the joint through available motion.
Splinting / flexion glove / TheraBand loopProvide positioning or controlled stretch for restricted joint motion; TheraBand loop is highlighted for PIP contractures.
Scar managementUltrasound, silicone and scar massage are among lecture-listed interventions; scar adhesions can restrict tendon glide.

Mechanism model: immobilization or scar adherence → reduced tissue excursion/joint motion → difficulty opening the hand or gripping → progressive, condition-appropriate ROM program.

EXAM TRAP

Do not equate AROM, AAROM and PROM. They differ in who provides the moving force and the patient’s active contribution.

RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · Why could a patient remain stiff after a successful volar-plate repair?

Healing, immobilization and scar/tissue restriction can reduce available PIP joint motion; an assessment should distinguish these from pain and edema.

OT FOR HAND PROBLEMS · 04

Strength: dose the type of contraction to the task

The lecture lists isometrics, concentric and eccentric exercise and multiple strengthening devices: Thera-putty, TheraBands, Digi-Flex, Thera-web, and Thera-bar.

Translate the terminology

  • Isometric: muscle force with no appreciable joint motion.
  • Concentric: muscle shortens under load.
  • Eccentric: muscle controls a load while lengthening.

The functional progression is not merely heavier resistance: it is controlled loading that ultimately supports the specific grip, pinch, lift or work task.

BOARD / CLINICAL ENRICHMENT

Eccentric loading is commonly used in tendinopathy rehabilitation, but exercise selection and timing depend on the diagnosis, healing stage, and referral protocol.

RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · What kind of muscle contraction generates force while the joint angle stays approximately fixed?

An isometric contraction.

OT FOR HAND PROBLEMS · 05

Edema: swelling can itself impair motion and comfort

Dr. Hall emphasizes gentle compression (circumferential Coban wrapping, Tubigrip, edema gloves), elevated exercise (“edema pumping”), and contrast baths. Gentle counterpressure can relieve the aching associated with articular or interstitial swelling.

Mechanism model: fluid accumulation → tissue pressure/ache and mechanical resistance to joint motion → difficulty performing hand tasks. Edema control may improve both comfort and access to ROM work.

MUST KNOW

Compression is not simply strengthening or splinting; its primary goal here is edema control and related symptom relief.

RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · What does “edema pumping” mean in this lecture?

Performing movement/exercise with the extremity elevated to assist swelling reduction.

OT FOR HAND PROBLEMS · 06

Sensation, coordination and dexterity: adapt when feedback is disrupted

Central or peripheral nerve damage may alter sensory input needed for hand control. The lecture names nerve gliding, ultrasound modalities and splint positioning as potential strategies, and emphasizes compensatory strategies such as visual guidance and repeated practice when sensation is deficient.

Why function changes: the hand depends on sensory feedback to adjust grip force and position. With poor sensation, the patient may drop an object, apply excessive force or fail to detect an unsafe contact.

FOUNDATIONS LINK

Sensory afferent information helps tune voluntary motor output; reduced feedback compromises the precision of fine-motor tasks.

RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · How could a patient compensate for impaired tactile feedback while picking up small objects?

Use vision deliberately to monitor finger position and practice the task repetitively with adapted tools or positioning when needed.

OT FOR HAND PROBLEMS · 07

Splinting: protect, stretch, and make the plan wearable

In the lecture, many upper-extremity splints are custom-made thermoplastic orthoses with hook-and-loop closures. Construction should account for the structure being protected, the tissue being stretched or stressed, and comfort to support adherence.

Clinical distinction: a protective orthosis limits motion that could jeopardize healing; a stretching orthosis supplies controlled force to address contracture. Off-the-shelf devices may be useful, particularly when hardware and thermoplastic elements provide static progressive tension.

COMMON CONFUSION

“Splint” does not automatically mean complete rest. Depending on the goal, an orthosis may protect a repair, position the limb, or apply controlled progressive stretch.

RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · What three priorities guide selection/fabrication of a hand orthosis in this lecture?

Protect the required structures; stretch/stress the intended structures; maximize comfort and adherence.

OT FOR HAND PROBLEMS · 08

Adaptive equipment: independence can improve before impairment resolves

For progressive disorders, the lecture recommends pairing compensation with remediation. A person with arthritis may have impaired grip strength and difficulty opening containers. Jar-opening aids reduce the physical demand of the activity while pain, strength and other deficits are treated.

Complex cases may require coordinated ordering/programming of sophisticated adaptive devices, including a robotic hand, with orthotics representatives.

CLINICAL CONNECTION

A meaningful outcome is whether someone can prepare a meal, work or participate in a valued activity—not merely the maximum grip strength measured in clinic.

RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · Why recommend a jar opener when the plan already includes hand strengthening?

The device can immediately improve independence while strengthening and symptom-control work proceed.

OT FOR HAND PROBLEMS · 09

Interprofessional workflow and physician communication

  1. Patient develops functional difficulty and consults PCP or orthopedic surgeon.
  2. Physician refers to OT.
  3. OT evaluates the patient and documents a plan.
  4. OT sends the plan to the physician for signed approval.
  5. Treatment begins with ongoing informal and periodic formal reassessment.
  6. Unexpected findings or recovery deviations are communicated promptly to the referring physician.

Dr. Hall states that OT must have a prescription to treat. For postsurgical care, surgeon and therapist typically agree on a rehabilitation protocol ahead of time, with individualized adjustments as needed. Nonsurgical care may be more iterative as symptoms localize and patient response becomes clearer.

Lecture example: wrist pain that decreases from 6/10 to 4/10 and becomes localized to the first dorsal compartment, together with a positive Finkelstein test, prompts the OT to communicate concern for de Quervain tenosynovitis and request advice about continued conservative care. This is clinical observation and collaboration—not an independent change in the physician’s diagnosis.

MUST KNOW

The physician–OT relationship includes referral, approval of the plan, protocol-based rehabilitation when appropriate, and communication when recovery differs from expectations.

RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · When should an OT contact the referring physician during rehabilitation?

When the patient has a significant status change or deviates from the anticipated recovery trajectory; the plan is coordinated with the physician.

OT FOR HAND PROBLEMS · 10

Apply it: the lecture’s finger, hand, wrist and elbow cases

Finger: 29-year-old after repaired volar plate injury

Four months after left middle-finger injury/repair and immobilization, only two therapy visits were possible because of social factors; a PIP flexion contracture developed. The first assessment should address all five domains, particularly ROM and scar/soft tissue limitations. In the lecture framework, consider controlled stretching/orthosis options, scar treatment, pain/edema control and task-focused home work within the surgeon’s protocol.

Finger: 67-year-old with rheumatoid arthritis and boutonnière deformity

The case gives PIP flexion with DIP hyperextension. Hall associates this with central-slip injury/deterioration and describes the Elson test with the PIP fixed in 90° flexion; the lecture states an extended/rigid DIP is a positive test, while a lax DIP is negative. Address deformity and function with the proper orthotic plan and physician coordination.

Hand: after carpal tunnel release

A 67-year-old reports persistent proximal palmar/radial-pillar pain at 2-, 6-, and 12-week follow-ups. Evaluate pain, edema, ROM, strength and sensation/dexterity; interventions depend on findings and surgical guidance.

Hand: 75-year-old with arthritis and weakness

Dr. Hall notes possible combined OA/RA and stresses inflammation control, rest, heat/cold and gentle ROM and strengthening. Do not work through pain. Functional aids may help; the slide raises physician referral for possible LRTI as a consideration rather than a universal recommendation.

Wrist: 55-year-old housekeeper with pain

Investigate work tasks (6–8 hours of cleaning per day), repetitive forces, symptom location, severity and occupation demands; assess the five domains and customize treatment to the work exposure. The slide includes images suggestive of radial wrist pain; do not assume a final diagnosis without examination.

Wrist: distal radius ORIF in a landscaper

A 34-year-old needs to regain both power-tool and keyboard tasks. The slide asks for evaluation and a general rehabilitation timeline using the supplied postoperative protocol; exact milestones are not stated on the slide and should not be invented.

Wrist: 54-year-old with osteoarthritis

The lecture frames approximately six weeks of conservative treatment as an opportunity to improve symptoms and function, with consideration of proximal-row carpectomy if there is no change; that is a specific example, not a universal surgical threshold.

Elbow: tennis-related pain, pediatric fracture, rheumatoid arthritis

A retired tennis player with intermittent recurrent elbow pain needs assessment of occupational loading and a graded recovery strategy. A nine-year-old after supracondylar fracture/cast removal needs progressive recovery of motion, strength and function before safe gymnastics return, following surgeon clearance. A 45-year-old with RA exacerbation requires supportive, symptom-sensitive therapy and close communication with rheumatology.

COMMON CONFUSION

Boutonnière (PIP flexion + DIP hyperextension) is not the same as swan-neck (PIP hyperextension + DIP flexion). The former is the case explicitly shown in this lecture.

RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · Which combination indicates the boutonnière pattern, and what tissue is implicated?

PIP flexion plus DIP hyperextension, associated in this lecture with central-slip deterioration/injury.

RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · Why is the housekeeper’s occupation important to the treatment plan?

Repetitive hand/wrist loading, hours, task demands and ability to modify tasks influence both symptoms and realistic rehabilitation goals.

MASTER THESE BEFORE MOVING ON

  1. Five-domain assessment. Pain, ROM, strength, edema, sensation/coordination/dexterity explain why a person cannot do a task and direct therapy.
  2. Remediation versus compensation. Exercises and symptom treatment address impairment; adaptive tools may restore function before the impairment fully resolves.
  3. Splint purpose. Protect versus controlled stretching; prioritize structures, fit and adherence.
  4. Interprofessional care. Referral, evaluation, physician-signed plan, agreed postoperative protocol and two-way communication guide safe recovery.
  5. Case-driven adaptation. Volar-plate contracture, boutonnière deformity, postsurgical pillar pain, arthritis and occupational overuse require different functional priorities.

THE MOST USEFUL FIRST AID CONNECTIONS

FIRST AID CONNECTION: Carpal tunnel syndrome involves median nerve compression and may require postsurgical rehabilitation; de Quervain tenosynovitis produces radial wrist pain associated with first dorsal compartment tendons; RA can affect hand function via inflammatory joint disease. These connections support the slide examples and are not additional lecture treatment protocols.

Source: Meghan V. Hall, MHS, OTR/L, The Hand, Wrist, & Elbow: OT Intervention, 25 slides. Images are embedded from the supplied lecture. External or clinical additions are labeled.
